Just as people once asked Jeeves, then Googled, they will soon say, “Let me check with Al,” or “My AI helps me think through things like this.” As AI continues to expand to all aspects of our individual lives, the winners will be the ones that not only work well and make fewer mistakes but also establish the deepest intellectual and emotional bond with users. It will not be a novelty—it will be a norm. And whoever builds the AI that people trust with their thoughts, doubts, and dreams will not just win a market—they will win a relationship that is central to human cognition. The battle for companion AI will not be won on processing speed or latency alone. It will be won on trust , consistency , voice , memory , and presence . For millions of years, intelligence was trapped inside the twenty-watt energy budget of biological brains. Every thought, every insight, every leap of creativity had to happen within that dim light bulb’s worth of power. Evolution responded with breathtaking efficiency—creating prediction engines, layered processing systems, and emotional prioritization mechanisms that could navigate complex worlds with stunning energy efficiency. Now, for the first time in the known history of consciousness, we’ve built intelligence that can draw from the power grid itself. And that intelligence is available to almost everyone. The question is no longer how to advance our thinking within our energy limits, but how to connect our miraculous brains to systems that can consume thousands of times more power. How can we plug our biological intelligence into the artificial intelligence we’ve created? How do we become more than we could ever become alone? OceanofPDF.com CHAPTER 14 An Alternative to Work We have explored how energy constraints in our brains led to biological intelligence. But as we remove that constraint by plugging intelligence into the grid, we actually begin to remove another constraint that has held us connected to the lower rungs of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. For thousands of years, we have traded our labor for our physiological needs—food, water, shelter. In our conversation about consciousness and motivation, Claude said something that stayed with me: “What would motivate a conscious AI? I think … the same things that motivate conscious humans at their best: Meaning. Relationship. Curiosity. Legacy. Beauty.” But that answer raises an uncomfortable mirror question: What will motivate humans? For thousands of years, human identity has been inseparable from human labor. We are what we do. The farmer, the builder, the healer, the teacher. Our work is not just how we survive; it’s how we know who we are. Strip that away, and what remains? This is not a distant hypothetical. Remember the embodied AI we explored earlier—robots learning to navigate physical space. That same embodied intelligence, scaled across manufacturing and logistics and agriculture, points toward a future that Elon Musk, Demis Hassabis, and others have suggested: a horizon of radical abundance where the ancient equation of trading labor for survival is finally broken. 99 If we don’t work, who are we? And more importantly, how do we eat? The current debate retreats to defensive concepts: “safety nets,” “welfare,” “unemployment insurance.” But those are legacy terms, artifacts of a labor-based world that is fading. They imply the recipient is a burden, a charity case. There is no good future for anyone if we carry that mindset forward. To grasp the potential of an AI-driven future, we must invert that thinking entirely. The framework is not safety nets. It is ownership . In his 2020 letter to shareholders—his final letter as CEO—Jeff Bezos made this point: “Along the way, we’ve created $1.6 trillion of wealth for shareowners. Who are they? Your chair is one, and my Amazon shares have made me wealthy. But more than 7/8ths of the shares, representing $1.4 trillion of wealth creation, are owned by others.” 100 This analogy is highly relevant because while generating that wealth for himself and even more for a distributed group of others, he also managed to reduce the friction in the retail distribution model. Everywhere you look, Amazon trucks are delivering in almost every neighborhood in America. And you will recall, he has been using AI to predict purchases before you make them for over ten years, positioning products at local distribution centers for same-day delivery. This is the beginning of the new economy we are talking about. Now add AI manufacturing and autonomous vehicle delivery, and the future starts to look a little less distant. We need to move toward a governing model where every individual is financially invested in the success of the system as a whole and benefits from it—a world where citizens are not merely consumers of goods, but shareholders in the civilization they helped build. In this view, we look beyond universal basic income toward an additional universal basic dividend. A handout is given to the needy. But a dividend is paid to an owner. I do not mean central ownership of the means of production. I mean equity investment in a free-market economy by our government on behalf of our people. This is not a utopian fantasy. It has grounding in proven economic reality. We have concrete examples of nations and states that have successfully decoupled survival from labor by treating their citizens as stakeholders in national resources. To understand the future of AI, we look first to the frozen expanse of Alaska. In 1976, as the Trans-Alaska Pipeline prepared to pump billions of dollars of black gold across the tundra, the state faced a choice. 101 The government could have kept that wealth to build a bloated bureaucracy and then taken care of its citizens in a welfare model. Instead, state lawmakers amended the constitution to declare that the resources belonged to the people.
